elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once in any 12-month period.
elements.evidence: The clause limits audits to once “per year,” which does not establish a rolling 12-month restriction.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 30 days' written notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: Only 15 days’ prior notice is required, and the notice is not required to be written.
The clause contains no business-hours limitation.

elements.element: Audits are conducted by an independent auditor.
elements.evidence: Audits must be exercised through the F&ASC, but the clause does not require an independent auditor.

elements.element: The auditor is bound by confidentiality obligations.
elements.evidence: No confidentiality obligation applicable to the auditor or F&ASC is stated.

elements.element: Audits are conducted off-site where possible.
elements.evidence: The clause contains no off-site audit requirement or preference.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 5 percent.
elements.evidence: For a Vendor-requested audit of Customer, the requesting Party must reimburse the audited Party’s entire reasonable compliance costs. No underpayment exception shifts those costs to Customer, which is more protective than a 5 percent threshold.

elements.element: Vendor has no direct access to Customer systems for an audit.
elements.evidence: The clause does not prohibit direct access to Customer systems.

elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once per year.
elements.evidence: The added language limits any audit right with respect to a Party to no more than once per year.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 15 days' notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: The added language requires not less than fifteen days’ prior notice to the audited Party.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 10 percent.
elements.evidence: For a Vendor-requested audit of Customer, the requesting Party must reimburse the audited Party’s entire reasonable compliance costs. No underpayment exception shifts those costs to Customer, which is more protective than a 10 percent threshold.
